name: Alcohol and antibiotics: what the NHS says
headline: Can you drink alcohol with antibiotics? What the NHS says, and which ones differ
summary: It depends on the antibiotic: the NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with common ones, but firm warnings exist for a few.
keyPoints: The NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics, though alcohol may worsen side effects such as nausea or dizziness.
The NHS says to avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and tinidazole, and NHS 111 Wales names linezolid and doxycycline as antibiotics that alcohol can affect too.
The NHS says amoxicillin can be taken with alcohol, and that azithromycin can too unless it causes dizziness, although the About azithromycin page is more cautious.
UK sources word the advice differently, so the NHS points to a pharmacist or GP for a specific antibiotic.
For a serious allergic reaction to an antibiotic, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about drinking alcohol with antibiotics?
body.body:
The NHS says that drinking alcohol in moderation is unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics. It adds that some antibiotics can cause side effects such as feeling sick or dizzy, and alcohol may make these worse. So the answer depends on which antibiotic has been prescribed.

Antibiotics are medicines that treat infections caused by bacteria. The NHS interactions page says a GP or pharmacist can confirm whether a particular antibiotic is suitable to take with alcohol.

body.heading: Which antibiotics have a specific alcohol warning?
body.body:
A small number of antibiotics carry a firmer warning about alcohol. The NHS says to avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and with tinidazole. NHS 111 Wales says it may be best to avoid alcohol with linezolid, and says alcohol can affect how doxycycline works.

For linezolid, NHS 111 Wales names undistilled fermented drinks such as wine, beer, sherry and lager. For doxycycline, the NHS common questions page says it is best not to drink alcohol, because alcohol can stop the medicine working properly.

body.heading: What can happen if alcohol is mixed with metronidazole?
body.body:
The NHS says that mixing alcohol with metronidazole can cause nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, hot flushes, a racing heartbeat and headache. Its common questions page says not to drink alcohol while using metronidazole tablets, liquid or suppositories.

The NHS says the advice to avoid alcohol carries on for a period after treatment finishes. NHS 111 Wales gives a longer period for tinidazole than for metronidazole. Apart from alcohol, the NHS says metronidazole users can eat and drink normally.

body.heading: Can alcohol make antibiotic side effects worse?
body.body:
Some antibiotics cause nausea or dizziness, and the NHS says alcohol may make these effects worse. The NHS lists dizziness as a common side effect of azithromycin.

For azithromycin, the NHS common questions page says that if the medicine makes a person dizzy, alcohol will make them feel worse. The NHS clarithromycin page gives the same caution about dizziness.

body.heading: What do the NHS pages say about amoxicillin and azithromycin?
body.body:
Amoxicillin belongs to the penicillin family of antibiotics, and azithromycin to the macrolide family. The NHS common questions page for amoxicillin says alcohol can be drunk while taking it, and that no food or drink needs to be avoided.

For azithromycin, the NHS common questions page says alcohol can be drunk, but not if the medicine causes dizziness. The About azithromycin page is stricter and says not to drink alcohol because it will make a person feel worse. The NHS common questions pages for flucloxacillin and ciprofloxacin also say alcohol can be drunk. The wording differs between pages for the same medicine, so a pharmacist can say how it applies to a particular prescription.

body.heading: Do all UK health sources give the same advice?
body.body:
They do not always match. NHS inform, the Scottish NHS information service, says alcohol should not be drunk while taking antibiotics, or for a period after finishing them. The NHS interactions page is more relaxed about moderate drinking with common antibiotics, then names metronidazole and tinidazole as exceptions.

NHS 111 Wales lists the antibiotics with firmer warnings and says it is a good idea to ask a GP or pharmacist if unsure.

body.heading: Who can give advice, and when is it urgent?
body.body:
For a question about one antibiotic and alcohol, the NHS points to a pharmacist or GP. The NHS says that in very rare cases an allergic reaction to an antibiotic can lead to anaphylaxis, which is a medical emergency.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a skin rash, wheezing, tightness in the chest or throat, trouble breathing or talking, or swelling of the mouth, face, lips, tongue or throat. For less severe reactions, an Oxford University Hospitals leaflet points to a GP or NHS 111.
